summary: Explains how an LDAPv2 client, which does not understand referrals, can work with the Common Indexing Protocol's index mesh, which depends heavily on them. It defines one possible way to handle this. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: An old phone book app does not know how to say go ask someone else. This describes a workaround so it still works.

questions: how do ldapv2 clients work with cip
how does a client search an index mesh
what is the extended dsi attribute
subtitle: Bridging old LDAP clients to a referral-aware index mesh.

tldr.problem: LDAPv2 clients do not understand referrals, but the Common Indexing Protocol's mesh depends on referrals to route queries efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines object classes and attributes that represent an index mesh as a directory tree that LDAPv2 clients can navigate. The mesh appearance uses defined structures (cIPIndex, cIPDataSet object classes and related attributes) allowing clients to search for index values, discover which datasets might contain answers, and query those datasets.
tldr.outcome: Experimental. Provides a workaround for integrating legacy LDAPv2 clients into a CIP mesh, though it adds complexity to clients.

today: RFC 2657 is Experimental. It was designed to help LDAPv2 clients work with CIP, but CIP itself saw limited deployment, making this integration method largely unused in practice.

sections.title: The Integration Problem
sections.content:
RFC 2657 solves a compatibility problem. The Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) relies on servers passing referrals to route queries: server A tells a client go ask server B about this. But LDAPv2, an older directory protocol (RFC 1777), has no notion of referrals. Clients built for LDAPv2 cannot follow them.

Rather than change LDAPv2 clients, this RFC proposes adding intelligence to them by representing the index mesh as a single LDAP directory tree, complete with object classes and attributes that describe the mesh structure and indexes. This allows LDAPv2 clients to navigate the mesh through LDAP searches and queries instead of through referrals.
sections.eli5: Old clients do not know how to follow instructions to go elsewhere. So instead of telling them to go elsewhere, you make it look like the other place is part of the directory they are already searching.

sections.title: CIP Object Classes and Attributes
sections.content:
Two object classes represent the mesh: cIPDataSet (one per indexed dataset) and cIPIndex (one per index value). A cIPDataSet entry holds information about what a particular index server has indexed: the dataset identifier (dSI), the search base within that dataset, and optionally a description, index type, and protocol version. A cIPIndex entry holds a single index value (stored in the idx attribute) along with extendedDSI values that list which datasets contain resources matching that index value.

Other attributes define URIs for supplier and consumer servers, update intervals, security options, and attribute namespace agreements. Together, these attributes allow clients to discover indexes, identify relevant datasets, and determine how to query the underlying data sources.
sections.eli5: One type of directory entry describes a dataset (what is indexed and where). Another describes an index value (what data contains this value). The attributes say who supplies the data, how often it updates, and what comes next.

sections.title: Client Navigation
sections.content: A client finds a suitable index mesh by searching for entries of class cIPDataSet at some base in the DIT. Each result describes an available index via a human-readable description and the indexOCAT attribute (which states the object class and attribute being indexed, like person cn). The client chooses an index that matches the search goal. To find matching resources, the client searches within that index's base for entries matching the desired index value (using the idx attribute). Each matching index entry contains extendedDSI values listing dataset identifiers where resources with that value exist. The client then queries those datasets by their identifiers, deriving the appropriate search filter from the indexOCAT information. Finally, the client queries the actual end servers holding the original data.
sections.eli5: First you ask the directory which indexes exist. Then you search an index for the value you want. That tells you which datasets might have it. Then you query those datasets. Finally you reach the actual data.

sections.title: Example Search Session
sections.content:
The RFC includes a complete example: searching for the email address of Roland Hedberg at Umea University in Sweden. The client searches for available indexes under c=SE with the filter (objectclass=cipDataset). Two indexes are returned: one covering all Swedish higher education employees, one covering Swedish lawyers. The client chooses the first. It then searches that index's base for index values matching Roland or Hedberg, and receives back extendedDSI values pointing to four datasets. By comparing which datasets appear in both results, the client narrows to two likely candidates: Umea University and Lund University. A final query on the Umea University dataset yields Roland Hedberg's record with his email address.

This multi-step process emulates what a referral-aware CIP client would do in a single transaction, but without ever requiring the LDAPv2 client to understand referrals.
sections.eli5: Find the university index. Search it for Roland and Hedberg. See which universities have both. Pick Umea. Search Umea's directory for the full name. Get the email.
